clinicalPearls: Common, benign, non-epileptic paroxysmal events of infants and toddlers, with peak occurrence between 6 and 18 months and usual resolution by 5-6 years of age
Two main types are recognised: cyanotic (blue) spells triggered by anger, frustration or vigorous crying, and pallid (white) spells triggered by pain, sudden fright or minor injury

The typical sequence is a provoking stimulus, then crying, then breath held in expiration, then colour change and limpness with possible brief loss of consciousness; prolonged spells may end in a few tonic-clonic movements (a reflex anoxic seizure)
Pallid spells are mediated by a vagally driven cardiac asystole or profound bradycardia, whereas cyanotic spells involve prolonged expiratory apnoea with altered respiratory control
Recovery is rapid and spontaneous with prompt return to normal activity, and there is no prolonged postictal confusion as seen with epilepsy
Iron deficiency, with or without anaemia, is a recognised association and iron supplementation reduces spell frequency in many children
Diagnosis is clinical from a clear temporal and eyewitness account; investigations are usually unnecessary, though an ECG helps exclude a long QT or arrhythmia mimic in atypical cases
Management centres on parental reassurance and education, avoiding reinforcement of the behaviour, with the clear message that spells do not cause brain damage and are not epilepsy
reference.pathophysiology: Breath-holding spells reflect dysregulated autonomic control in an immature nervous system. In cyanotic spells, provoked crying leads to prolonged expiratory apnoea with hypoxaemia and cerebral hypoxia, causing loss of consciousness and occasionally a reflex anoxic seizure. In pallid spells, a noxious stimulus triggers an exaggerated vagal reflex producing transient cardiac asystole or profound bradycardia with cerebral hypoperfusion. Iron deficiency may contribute through its effects on neurotransmitter function and autonomic regulation, and a familial predisposition is common.
additionalDifferentials: Epileptic seizures, particularly tonic or atonic seizures
Cardiac arrhythmia including long QT syndrome and other causes of reflex anoxic syncope
Brainstem or posterior fossa lesion causing central apnoea
Gastro-oesophageal reflux with apnoea, or a brief resolved unexplained event
Central hypoventilation or other disorder of respiratory control
additionalInvestigations: Detailed eyewitness account confirming the typical trigger-and-sequence pattern
Full blood count with ferritin and iron studies to detect iron deficiency
ECG to exclude long QT syndrome or arrhythmia in atypical, pallid or severe cases
EEG only if the diagnosis is uncertain or seizures are strongly suspected
Echocardiography or cardiology referral if a cardiac cause is suspected
Developmental and growth assessment to confirm an otherwise normal child
redFlags: Events without a clear provoking trigger, or occurring during sleep
Prolonged loss of consciousness, focal neurological features or a true postictal state
Family history of sudden cardiac death, or syncope on exertion or startle suggesting long QT syndrome
Developmental regression or an abnormal interictal neurological examination
Onset in the newborn period or persistence well beyond the expected age
reference.prognosis: The outlook is excellent; spells resolve spontaneously in almost all children by school age with no long-term neurological sequelae. A minority of children with pallid spells develop vasovagal syncope in later life.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing spells as epilepsy and initiating antiepileptic drugs
Failing to check for and treat iron deficiency
Missing an underlying long QT syndrome or arrhythmia in atypical or unprovoked events
Alarming parents unnecessarily, or conversely dismissing genuinely atypical events without an ECG
Reinforcing the behaviour by altering normal discipline for fear of provoking spells
references: Swaiman's Pediatric Neurology: Principles and Practice
management: Reassure and educate parents that spells are benign, non-epileptic, and self-limiting, resolving by school age
Give oral iron supplementation when iron deficiency is present, even without anaemia, as it reduces spell frequency
Advise first-aid measures during a spell: lay the child flat, protect from injury, and avoid shaking or unnecessary resuscitation
Coach consistent, calm behavioural management of triggering tantrums without reinforcing the episodes
Obtain an ECG to exclude long QT syndrome and refer to cardiology in atypical, severe, or pallid spells
Reserve referral for further evaluation, and rarely cardiac pacing, for frequent, severe pallid spells with prolonged asystole
